title: What Arab Israelis Really Think About Israel’s Election
gist: Survey data show Arab citizens of Israel prioritize crime over Palestine (74% vs 7.6%) and 77% want an Arab party in the next coalition. Ra'am's Mansour Abbas, allied with ex-police chief Yoav Segalovitz, is pitching itself as a kingmaker in an October election where neither camp is expected to reach 61 seats, even as the elections committee voted to disqualify Arab parties.

insights.claim: 74 percent of Arab citizens of Israel say violence and crime is their biggest concern versus 7.6 percent citing resolution of the Israel-Palestine conflict.
insights.speaker: Anchal Vohra
insights.so_what: Shows a pragmatic, domestically focused Arab electorate open to coalition politics.
insights.quote: Seventy-four percent of respondents said violence and crime was their biggest concern, while 7.6 percent noted the importance of resolving the Israel-Palestine crisis
insights.locator: What is the biggest election issue

insights.claim: 77 percent of Arab Israelis support including an Arab party in the next governing coalition.
insights.speaker: Anchal Vohra
insights.so_what: Supports the feasibility of an Arab-backed coalition if Jewish parties accept it.
insights.quote: An overwhelming 77 percent support the inclusion of an Arab party in the next government’s coalition.

insights.claim: 241 Arabs were murdered in Israel last year compared with 47 Jews, per the Knesset's National Security Committee.
insights.speaker: Anchal Vohra
insights.so_what: Quantifies the crime gap driving Arab voter behavior.
insights.quote: 241 Arabs were murdered last year compared to 47 Jews

insights.claim: Neither opposition camp is expected to reach the 61 seats needed to govern, so Ra'am, projected at four to five seats, could prove instrumental again.
insights.speaker: Anchal Vohra
insights.so_what: Raises odds of a hung parliament and unusual coalition outcomes affecting Israeli policy direction.
insights.quote: Neither opposition camp is expected to gather the required 61 seats.

insights.claim: Israel's Central Elections Committee voted to disqualify Ra'am's United Arab List and the Joint List, but as in past elections the Supreme Court will likely reverse it.
insights.speaker: Anchal Vohra
insights.so_what: Disqualification is likely noise, but highlights institutional tension within Israeli democracy.
insights.quote: these decisions will likely be reversed

insights.claim: Gadi Eisenkot, seen as Netanyahu's toughest challenger, has not ruled out Ra'am in a coalition if it recognizes Israel as a Jewish and democratic state, a threshold Abbas and Segalovitz have met.
insights.speaker: Anchal Vohra
insights.so_what: Creates a plausible path for an anti-Netanyahu government.
insights.locator: Gadi Eisenkot, the leader of Yaashav

insights.claim: Ra'am recruited former top cop Yoav Segalovitz, whose Lahav 433 unit cut Arab-community homicides by 16 percent and shootings by 30 percent, before crime spiked to records under Itamar Ben-Gvir.
insights.speaker: Anchal Vohra
insights.so_what: Crime policy is a credible differentiator in the campaign.

insights.claim: The author argues an Arab party at the top of Israeli decision-making could soften Arab neighbors toward future normalization deals.
insights.speaker: Anchal Vohra
insights.so_what: A second-order path to Abraham Accords-style expansion.
insights.quote: A place for Palestinian Israelis at the very top of decision-making could potentially soften Israel’s Arab neighbors to future normalization deals.
